name: Phentermine

lead: Phentermine is a prescription stimulant that suppresses appetite and has been used for short-term weight loss since 1959. It is one of the most prescribed obesity drugs in the US and appears in many forum fat-loss stacks, aimed at lower body fat through eating less.

It is an amphetamine-like sympathomimetic amine that releases norepinephrine in the brain, which reduces hunger. Weight loss is modest, about 3.6 kg more than placebo at 12 weeks per one summary, and smaller than with newer incretin drugs. It is also one half of Qsymia (phentermine/topiramate).

paras: It is taken as a short-term adjunct, usually described as a few weeks, alongside diet, exercise and behavior change. Brands include Adipex-P, Lomaira and Duromine.

Labels warn of rare pulmonary hypertension and valvular heart disease, and of raised blood pressure, insomnia and dependence-related withdrawal. It is a controlled substance and contraindicated in pregnancy. The 1990s fen-phen combination was linked to heart valve damage, which led to fenfluramine's withdrawal.

angle.text: Phentermine is a decades-old prescription appetite suppressant used for short-term weight loss and cutting. It cuts hunger so you eat less and lose body fat. Trials show modest loss over weeks to months, and it appears in many forum fat-loss stacks.

lead: Phentermine is a sympathomimetic amine with an amphetamine-like profile, sold by prescription as an appetite suppressant and approved in the US as a short-term adjunct, usually described as a few weeks, to diet, exercise and behavior change in adults with obesity [1][2]. For appearance, the route is direct: lower hunger makes a calorie deficit easier to hold, a deficit reduces body fat over weeks, and less body fat changes how the face, waist and whole physique look. Brands include Adipex-P, Lomaira, Ionamin and Duromine [2][3].

The US Food and Drug Administration approved phentermine in 1959, and it remains available as a generic; Wikipedia reports it was the 168th most commonly prescribed US medication in 2023, with more than 3 million prescriptions [3]. Reviews describe it as the commonly prescribed obesity drug, with modest average weight loss compared with newer incretin drugs; one summary cites about 3.6 kg more than placebo over 12 weeks [4][5][2]. It is also one of the two components of phentermine/topiramate (Qsymia), which was studied in the CONQUER, SEQUEL and EQUIP trials [6][7][8].

Phentermine is also remembered for the fenfluramine-phentermine (fen-phen) combination of the mid-1990s, which a 1997 report linked to valvular heart disease and which led to the withdrawal of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine [9][10][11]. Wikipedia states that the valve and pulmonary complications were attributed to the fenfluramine component rather than to phentermine, while the US label lists rare pulmonary hypertension and valvular heart disease among its warnings [3][1]. In bodybuilding and physique forums, phentermine is discussed as a prescription option for dieting and cutting phases, often alongside other drugs, and as a contrast with newer GLP-1 medications [12][13][14].
infobox: Sympathomimetic amine, anorectic; norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent [3]
Adipex-P, Lomaira, Ionamin, Duromine, Fastin; Qsymia (with topiramate) [3]
Short-term; approved for up to 12 weeks per Wikipedia [3]
Prescription-only; Schedule IV in the US, Class C in the UK [3]

paras: Appearance interest is in fat loss and appetite control. People use it to reduce body fat for a leaner face and body, and physique athletes discuss it for contest preparation or summer cuts [12][13]. The chain described by users is simple: appetite is quieter, eating less becomes manageable, and visible leanness follows, with some describing the effect as a way to keep thinking about food from dominating the day [14][12].

Forum posters also describe it as a way to help cardio output or drive during a diet, one saying a doctor-prescribed phentermine helped a little with cardio [15]. A Biggest-Loser discussion thread repeats an anecdote of a co-worker who combined appetite-suppressant injections and phentermine and lost weight quickly [16]. Others in the same communities say they prefer to avoid stimulant weight-loss drugs [17].

The label indicates phentermine as a short-term adjunct in weight reduction for patients with an initial BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with risk factors such as controlled hypertension, diabetes or hyperlipidemia [1]. Wikipedia describes approval for up to 12 weeks, with most weight loss in the first weeks and slower loss continuing in some studies for months [3]. Grokipedia states that longer off-label use has been studied and that prescribing to adolescents has risen [2]. A 2024 JAMA review of adolescent obesity covers pharmacotherapy options for young people [18].

The American Gastroenterological Association guideline on obesity pharmacotherapy and reviews in JAMA place phentermine among the generic, low-cost options alongside newer injectable and combination drugs [19][20][4]. The CDC reports that 41.9 percent of US adults had obesity in 2017 to March 2020, the population for whom these medications are mainly developed [21].

The FDA approved phentermine in 1959 as an appetite suppressant; hydrochloride and resin-bound forms were later marketed, which is the origin of brand names such as Adipex-P and Ionamin [3]. The name is a contraction of phenyl-tertiary-butyl amine, and chemically the drug is alpha,alpha-dimethylphenethylamine, an amphetamine derivative with an additional methyl group at the alpha carbon [3].

Combining fenfluramine with phentermine was studied in a double-blind trial from the University of Rochester published in 1984, which Wikipedia summarizes as showing greater weight loss with the combination than with placebo (8.4 kg versus 4.4 kg) and fewer adverse effects [11]. Fenfluramine had been sold since the 1970s with modest success until the pairing was heavily marketed in the 1990s; the shorthand fen-phen is credited by Wikipedia to Pietr Hitzig and Richard Rothman in 1994, who proposed the combination for alcohol and cocaine craving [11].

Wyeth introduced dexfenfluramine (Redux) in 1995 and the FDA approved it in 1996 [11]. In August 1997, clinicians at the Mayo Clinic described 24 women with unusual valvular heart disease associated with fenfluramine-phentermine in the New England Journal of Medicine [9]. The FDA asked in September 1997 that fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine be voluntarily withdrawn, and later work found abnormal valve findings in nearly 30 percent of people who had taken fenfluramine or dexfenfluramine for up to 24 months [3][11]. A 2000 Circulation paper proposed that activation of serotonin 5-HT2B receptors by fenfluramine-type drugs could explain the valvulopathy [10].

Wikipedia reports that more than 50,000 product-liability lawsuits were filed against Wyeth by 2005 and that liability estimates reached into the billions of dollars [11]. Phentermine alone remained on the US market. Wikipedia adds that it was withdrawn from the UK market in 2000 [3].

Vivus developed phentermine combined with extended-release topiramate, first called Qnexa and later Qsymia; Wikipedia credits the idea to Thomas Najarian, who used the combination off-label at a weight clinic in Los Osos, California, opened in 2001 [3]. The FDA declined to approve the combination in October 2010, citing a lack of long-term data and concerns about heart rate, cardiovascular events and birth defects; after resubmission, it became available in the US in 2012 and was approved with a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy, while the European Union declined approval later that year [22][3]. At the time of approval, one obesity specialist estimated that about 70 percent of colleagues were already prescribing the combination off-label, according to Wikipedia [3].

Network meta-analyses and reviews of obesity drugs include phentermine, usually combined with topiramate, among the available options and show smaller average weight loss than semaglutide or tirzepatide [5][4][23][24]. A 2025 network meta-analysis in Nature Medicine of 56 trials counted two for phentermine/topiramate, found all included drugs produced more weight loss than placebo, and reported over 10% total body weight loss for semaglutide and tirzepatide [25]. Because most phentermine trials are short, long-term outcomes of phentermine alone are less documented than those of the combination product [24][3].

For phentermine/topiramate, Wikipedia reports that patients at the highest dose lost 10 to 11 percent of body weight in trials versus 1 to 2 percent on placebo, and that 62 to 70 percent reached at least 5 percent loss at week 56 compared with 17 to 21 percent on placebo [22]. Wikipedia also notes that most weight loss with phentermine occurs in the first weeks, with a slower decline continuing through about nine months in some studies [3].

The CONQUER phase 3 trial tested two doses of low-dose controlled-release phentermine plus topiramate against placebo [6]; SEQUEL followed participants for two years [7]; EQUIP studied severely obese adults [8]. A 2025 trial analyzed predictors of BMI reduction on phentermine/topiramate in adolescents [26], and a 2021 trial compared it with exenatide and dapagliflozin in polycystic ovary syndrome [27].

Registered studies include a 600-person trial of intermittent phentermine with body composition outcomes, a long-term effectiveness study of 870 participants, a 92-person trial in patients undergoing bariatric surgery and a 13-person pilot on eating behavior [28][29][30][31]. A phase 2 trial in teens has been registered [32]. A pharmacokinetic study characterized steady-state levels of extended-release capsules [33].

Wikipedia lists common effects as palpitations, fast heart rate, raised blood pressure, restlessness, insomnia, tremor, dizziness, headache, dry mouth, nausea, constipation and diarrhea, with rare reports of stroke, heart attack, euphoria followed by fatigue, and very rarely psychosis [3]. The label lists primary pulmonary hypertension and valvular heart disease among warnings and states that co-administration with other weight-loss drugs is not recommended because safety and efficacy of combinations have not been established [1].

Contraindications described in the label and by Wikipedia include pregnancy and breastfeeding, a history of drug abuse, cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors within 14 days, and allergy to sympathomimetic amines [1][3]. Wikipedia says tolerance usually develops and describes dependence risk as low but not absent, listing abuse as a possible serious effect [3]. Phentermine/topiramate carries additional warnings, including birth-defect risk from topiramate, requirements for pregnancy testing in women of reproductive potential, and warnings on heart rate, mood and glaucoma [22].

Phentermine is described as a norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent with weak reuptake inhibition; its effects are mainly noradrenergic and its serotonergic activity is weak [3][34]. Amphetamine-type stimulants release norepinephrine more potently than dopamine or serotonin [34][2]. Wikipedia reports that phentermine is inactive at serotonin 5-HT2B receptors, which it contrasts with fenfluramine, and attributes the valve disease of fen-phen to fenfluramine [3][10]. The label states it has not been established that appetite suppression is the primary action [1].

Phentermine is rapidly absorbed orally with high bioavailability that a high-fat meal does not alter. About 6 percent is metabolized, and 62 to 85 percent is excreted unchanged in urine; the half-life is roughly 20 to 25 hours, shorter in acidic urine [3]. A trial characterized steady-state pharmacokinetics of extended-release capsules [33].

Phentermine is a prescription-only controlled substance: Schedule IV in the US and under the international Convention on Psychotropic Substances, Class C in the UK, Schedule IV in Canada and prescription-only (S4) in Australia, according to Wikipedia [3][2]. Wikipedia also lists it as Class B2 in Brazil and Class C in New Zealand, and states that it remains available as a single agent in most countries [3]. Amphetamine preparations, by contrast, are Schedule II in the US [3].

On T Nation, users describe phentermine as one of several appetite or energy aids. One poster who had tried ephedrine, phentermine and ADHD medications said GLP-1 drugs were the most effective at quieting constant thoughts about food [14]. Another thread describes a lifter whose spouse suggested a phentermine prescription to get leaner; the poster notes that muscular people can exceed BMI thresholds [12]. A coach in a separate thread said a client's cutting program would include TRT, an oral anabolic and phentermine with blood work monitored [13], and a user on TRT describes a doctor prescribing phentermine alongside it [35].

Opinion in the same forums is mixed. One user said they disliked the 'dirty feeling' of phentermine prescribed earlier [36]; another declined a doctor's suggestion of metabolism-speeding medication such as phentermine [17]. A 2006 poster who used a prescribed phentermine while trying to regain muscle after weight loss called it 'speed' [15].

Phentermine sits in the same family of appetite and fat-loss tools as ephedrine-caffeine stacks, ADHD stimulants and GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, which reviews report produce larger average weight loss [25][14].

lore.intro: On physique forums, phentermine appears as one of several appetite suppressants and stimulants discussed for dieting [12][14].

claims.claim: Phentermine makes a hard cut easier by shutting off hunger
It can be stacked with TRT and oral anabolics on a cut
It feels like speed and can be unpleasant
Phentermine is a safer relative of fen-phen
GLP-1 drugs have replaced phentermine for serious cutting
Prescription appetite suppression preserves a physique better than crash dieting

timeline.event: The FDA approves phentermine as an appetite suppressant [3].
A University of Rochester double-blind trial of fenfluramine plus phentermine is published [11].
The term fen-phen is coined, per Wikipedia, for treating alcohol and cocaine craving [11].
The NEJM reports valvular heart disease in 24 fenfluramine-phentermine users; fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine are withdrawn [9][3].
Phentermine is withdrawn from the UK market, per Wikipedia [3].
Thomas Najarian opens a California weight clinic where he uses phentermine/topiramate off-label [3].
The FDA declines to approve phentermine/topiramate over safety concerns [22][3].
The CONQUER trial of phentermine/topiramate is published [6].
Qsymia (phentermine/topiramate) is approved in the US; the EU declines approval [22].
More than 3 million US phentermine prescriptions, per Wikipedia [3].
